title: When AI Helps You Learn—and When It Only Helps You Finish
author: Keiffenheim, Eva
summary: Eva Keiffenheim examines the neuroscience of cognitive offloading to ask when generative AI strengthens learning and when it quietly erodes it. Because learning depends on activity-dependent plasticity, letting AI perform a cognitive process for us removes our own opportunity to practice that process, echoing prior findings on GPS use degrading spatial memory and the 'Google Effect' on recall. She organizes the risk around five interacting processes — attention, connection, productive effort, feedback, and retrieval — and argues AI can either strengthen or short-circuit each one depending on how it's used. The piece proposes a simple 'tool-off interval' safeguard: close the AI, reconstruct the idea from a blank page, solve a new problem unaided, then reopen the AI only to check and extend the work. It closes by reframing the real variable as which role AI plays (solver, tutor, testing partner, or copilot) rather than whether AI is used at all.
points: AI's frictionless ease is a red flag, not a green light: neuroplasticity requires practice, so having AI perform a cognitive process removes your chance to strengthen that exact process.
Prior research on GPS and the 'Google Effect' shows tools that reliably supply answers reduce what we remember about the content itself, only where to find it.
Use the five-part framework — Attention, Connection, Productive Effort, Feedback, Retrieval — to audit whether a given AI use strengthens or bypasses each stage of learning.
Build a 'tool-off interval' into study routines: close the AI, reconstruct the idea unaided, attempt a new problem, then reopen AI only to check and extend.

The determining factor isn't whether you use AI but which role it plays — solver (does the work for you), tutor (guides with hints), testing partner (creates retrieval practice), or copilot (supports the teacher).
quotes: Learning changes the brain through activity-dependent plasticity: practice alters the strength and organisation of neural networks.
when AI performs a cognitive process for us, we lose an opportunity to practise that process ourselves.
we know that by relying on GPS have poorer spatial-memory performance
Used poorly, AI can remove the productive effort through which knowledge becomes organised and usable.
Reading an AI-generated summary again is not the same as recalling the underlying ideas from memory.
Asking AI to explain something again is not the same as explaining it oneself.
AI is most likely to strengthen learning when it removes unnecessary friction while preserving—or deliberately eliciting—the learner’s core cognitive work
